title: The protection system
hook: the Khalsa offered villages protection in return for a share of the harvest

segments.voice: Yesterday, a minister's grief for his brother became a war on a whole people, and the Sikh memory of it carries the dead without a curse. Your line was grief without hate. Did a hurt try to turn into blame? Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

Harvest time in a Punjab village, in the hard years. The wheat is in. And everyone in the village knows what can happen next. Raiders from outside. A local strongman's men. Tax collectors who take far more than the tax. There's no police to call, and the government in Lahore is either far away or part of the problem. Then a group of Sikh horsemen rides in, and their leader makes an offer to the village elders. Pay us a share of the harvest, and no one touches this village. If anyone does, they answer to us. Today's word is the name of that offer: rakhi.
screen: `HARVEST IN.` → `NO ONE TO CALL.` → `AN OFFER AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Rakhi is a Punjabi word for guarding, keeping watch, protection. And in these years it became the name of a system. Tradition describes it like this. A Sikh band would take a village under its rakhi. The village paid a share of its crops at harvest. In return the band promised to keep the village safe from plunder, by anyone. Notice what that means for a community that, only a few years earlier, had been living on horseback in forests with a price on its head. The hunted were becoming the protectors. Tradition says villagers who had never taken amrit, Hindu and Muslim as well as Sikh, now looked to the Khalsa to keep their harvest safe. It isn't a simple story. Some readers see in rakhi an early shape of the Sikh states that would come later: protection, then loyalty, then land. Some point out that a band that collects a share for safety is holding real power over the village, and that power can be used well or badly. Sikh tradition remembers the ideal and measures the bands against it. Where does that ideal come from? The Sikh scripture keeps describing God as the one who protects, the keeper, the shelter of those who have no shelter. And Sikh teaching holds that the Khalsa is there to defend the weak. A line of Guru Arjan in the Granth, in paraphrase, says the Lord has become the protector, and no one can harm the one he keeps. Rakhi took that and made it an everyday job: walking a village's boundary, answering when someone called for help. Sikhs today don't collect a harvest share. But the job survives in a smaller shape: knowing your neighbors, and being someone they could come to. Keep the village safe.
screen: `RAKHI: GUARDING, PROTECTION.` · `A SHARE OF THE HARVEST FOR SAFETY.` · `THE HUNTED BECAME PROTECTORS.` · `POWER, USED WELL OR BADLY.` · then, large: `KEEP THE VILLAGE SAFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: protect one neighbor. Sit comfortably, and breathe. In your mind, walk the boundary of your own small village: your street, your building, your floor, your team. Who lives along it? Let faces come. Now notice one who might need a little looking after. Someone older, someone alone, someone new, someone having a hard month. Don't plan a rescue. Just pick one person, and one small way to keep watch: a knock, a message, a carried bag. If you pray, you can hold them in your mind and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Rakhi. Protection. The system in which Sikh bands guarded villages from plunder in return for a share of the harvest. Today's word.
Your line: keep the village safe. Today, do one small thing that makes your neighbor's day safer or easier, without being asked. Day eight hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the Khalsa's duty to protect the weak, and Sikh groups today organize practical help for neighbors in need, regardless of faith.

fork.setup: you're an elder in a Punjab village. raiders could come any harvest, and Lahore won't help. a Sikh band offers protection for a share of the crop. what do you do?
options: refuse, and hope the raiders pass you by.
accept, and take the village under their rakhi.
pay the raiders instead, to keep them away.
fork.reveal: tradition says villages accepted, and the Khalsa that had been hunted became the guard on the village boundary.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rakhi, guarding or protection; here the name of the eighteenth-century system of Sikh protection for villages.

trapdoor: what you thought: rakhi is just a word for protection.
what it means: it named a system in which Sikh bands guarded villages from plunder in return for a share of the harvest.
what a scholar hears: some historians see in rakhi an early shape of the later Sikh states, protection turning into loyalty and then into land.

notes: No share figure is given (often said to be a fifth of the produce, paid at the two harvests); no frequency is stated.
'Hindu and Muslim as well as Sikh' villagers under rakhi: confirm.

The paraphrased line of Guru Arjan ('the Lord has become the protector, and no one can harm the one he keeps') is not tied to one Ang; several shabads carry this sense. A Keeper may want to choose one and cite its Ang.
'The Khalsa was told it existed to defend the weak' summarizes common Sikh teaching rather than a single text; confirm wording.
The historians' view (rakhi as the seed of the misl states) is presented as one view among others; confirm.
